name: Flupentixol (Fluanxol)
summary: First-generation (typical) antipsychotic, used mainly as a maintenance treatment for schizophrenia—often as a long-acting depot injection. Not available in the US.
description: Flupentixol is a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic used primarily for chronic schizophrenia, especially when you want stable coverage with a depot (long-acting) injection. It’s a dopamine-blocking medication, so it can help with hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, but it also carries classic risks like extrapyramidal symptoms (stiffness, tremor, restlessness), prolactin elevation, and QT prolongation. It is not available in the United States and is not a first-line option in most modern guidelines compared with atypical antipsychotics.
patient_summary: Flupentixol is an older antipsychotic used mostly for long-term treatment of schizophrenia, often as a depot injection every few weeks so you don’t have to remember daily pills. It can help stabilize voices, paranoia, and disorganized thinking, but it can also cause stiffness, shaking, restlessness, and high prolactin (menstrual or sexual side effects). It can affect the heart’s rhythm and blood pressure and is not approved in the US. This is not a medication for everyday anxiety or sleep—this is a serious antipsychotic that needs close psychiatric follow-up.

metadata.fda_approval_year: Not applicable (not FDA-approved in the United States)

primary_indications: Schizophrenia (maintenance treatment, including long-acting depot formulation)

linked_conditions.context: Used as a maintenance antipsychotic for chronic schizophrenia, often after stabilization on oral therapy and then transition to depot for adherence.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to flupentixol, thioxanthenes, or any component of the formulation
Acute intoxication with alcohol, barbiturates, or opioids
CNS depression of any cause or coma
Severely agitated psychotic patients, psychoneurotic patients, or geriatric patients with confusion and/or agitation
Suspected or established subcortical brain damage
Severe cardiovascular disease or circulatory collapse
Liver damage or significant hepatic impairment
Concomitant use with large doses of hypnotics
Known QT prolongation, history of torsades de pointes, or use of other QT-prolonging drugs when risk is high
Use in catatonia (may worsen psychosis and increase risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

efficacy_response.percentage_value: Not precisely defined in modern comparative trials
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Clinical experience suggests similar antipsychotic efficacy to other first-generation depot agents when equivalent D2-blocking doses are used.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Flupentixol is not the newest antipsychotic on the block. When doses are optimized and injections are given on schedule, many people see steady improvement in hallucinations, paranoia, and disorganization over several weeks. It’s usually chosen for people who benefit from antipsychotic medication but struggle to take daily pills.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Clinical experience and guideline-based use of first-generation depot antipsychotics

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral bioavailability about 40%; depot formulation provides slow, sustained release from the muscle.
pharmacokinetics.onset: IM depot: 24–72 hours after injection; oral: initial symptom improvement generally within 1–2 weeks.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: 3–8 hours; depot: 4–7 days after injection
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Oral tablets: continuous effect with regular daily dosing
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Depot: 2–4 weeks per injection depending on dose and individual metabolism
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism via sulfoxidation and dealkylation; also undergoes glucuronidation; metabolites are inactive.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Mostly in feces as metabolites; small amount in urine.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Oral tablets can be taken with or without food; no major clinically relevant food effect noted.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Flupentixol is a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic used mainly for long-term treatment of schizophrenia, especially when depot injections are preferred to support adherence. It is not an anxiety or sleep medicine and is not available in the United States.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia (maintenance)}: Ongoing treatment of chronic schizophrenia once a person is stabilized, often with transition from oral tablets to depot injections.
Oral start, depot maintenance: Typically started orally to confirm tolerability, then switched to long-acting depot injections for more stable blood levels and adherence.
Relapse prevention: Helps reduce risk of relapse and rehospitalization in people with chronic psychotic illness when taken regularly.
off_label: Not commonly used for mood or anxiety disorders in modern practice
Not appropriate for catatonia or purely behavioral agitation in dementia

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Experiences with flupentixol vary a lot. Below are common themes from patients when the dose is in the usual maintenance range.

quotes: This isn’t an instant calm – it felt more like my thoughts slowly untangled over a few weeks.
The voices faded into the background instead of disappearing overnight.
I didn’t wake up ‘fixed,’ but I noticed I was less paranoid and less on edge after a couple of weeks.
Getting a shot every few weeks is a drag, but I don’t have to remember pills every day.
On injection weeks, my arm is sore but my mood and thinking stay more even.
I used to miss doses all the time; the depot keeps me covered so I’m not constantly crashing.
My legs felt like they needed to move all the time – sitting still was torture.
I noticed a fine tremor and stiffness when the dose got higher.
It helped my psychosis but made me feel stiff and robotic until we added an EPS med and adjusted the dose.
items.note: Stiffness, tremor, and inner restlessness (akathisia) are classic risks with first-generation antipsychotics and need active monitoring.

quotes: It calmed my thoughts but didn’t knock me out like some other antipsychotics.
I felt a bit slower mentally, but less overwhelmed by racing ideas.
On bad days I feel tired and flat; we had to fine-tune the dose so I could function.
My periods became irregular, and my libido dropped off.
I had some breast tenderness and leakage that freaked me out.
Sex drive and erection issues showed up after a while – we had to talk about prolactin.
items.note: Like many typical antipsychotics, flupentixol can raise prolactin, which can affect periods, breast tissue, and sexual function.

quotes: When I delayed my shot, paranoia started creeping back a week or two later.
Stopping the pills suddenly made me anxious and restless within a few days.
The depot wears off slowly, so I didn’t crash overnight, but I did relapse when I skipped appointments.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Flupentixol is not a ‘take it once and instantly feel better’ medication. It’s built for longer-term stabilization, especially in depot form.
key_points: Oral onset: Early improvement in agitation or psychotic symptoms may appear within 1–2 weeks.
Full effect: Continued improvement often unfolds over 4–6 weeks of consistent dosing.
Depot onset: Long-acting IM injection generally starts working 24–72 hours after a dose.
Depot duration: One injection can last about 2–4 weeks depending on dose and individual factors.
Half-life: Oral half-life is roughly 35 hours; depot half-life is about 3 weeks, so the drug leaves the body slowly.
Clinical reality: Because depot levels fade gradually, relapse tends to creep in over days to weeks rather than overnight if injections are missed.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Symptom improvement and relapse prevention in schizophrenia
sections.value: Clinically effective when dosed appropriately and maintained over time
sections.comparison: Generally comparable to other first-generation depot antipsychotics when using equivalent doses
sections.text: Flupentixol can be an effective maintenance antipsychotic for people with schizophrenia, particularly when adherence to daily tablets is difficult. Its value is less about being ‘stronger’ than other antipsychotics and more about providing steady dopamine blockade via long-acting injections. For many patients, staying on a consistent depot schedule reduces relapse rates, emergency visits, and rehospitalizations. Tradeoffs include a higher risk of movement side effects and prolactin elevation compared with many atypical antipsychotics.
sections.clinical_details: Evidence for flupentixol comes largely from older studies and clinical experience with first-generation depot antipsychotics. Typical response patterns include gradual reduction in hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought, often over 4–6 weeks. Depot formulations may improve adherence and reduce relapse risk compared with oral-only regimens, especially in patients with chronic illness and prior nonadherence. However, modern guidelines usually favor second-generation antipsychotics first due to a more favorable extrapyramidal symptom profile. Flupentixol is more commonly encountered in regions where it remains marketed and where cost, availability, or prior response drive antipsychotic selection.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This is a potent antipsychotic. It can affect heart rhythm, blood pressure, movement, temperature regulation, and hormones. It is NOT for routine anxiety or insomnia.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis who are treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Most deaths are cardiovascular or infectious. Flupentixol is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) has been reported with flupentixol and other antipsychotics and can be fatal. Monitor closely for fever, rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability and stop the medication immediately if NMS is suspected.
other: Cardiac conduction risk: May prolong QT interval and trigger serious arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes, especially in patients with heart disease, bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities, or other QT-prolonging medications.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Life-threatening reaction with fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability, and elevated CPK. Requires immediate discontinuation and emergency care.
Not for catatonia: Antipsychotics can worsen outcomes and increase NMS risk in catatonia. Benzodiazepines or ECT are preferred in that setting.
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): High risk of parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, and, with long-term use, tardive dyskinesia.
Metabolic effects: Can worsen glucose tolerance and cause diabetic ketoacidosis even in people without known diabetes. Monitor weight and metabolic parameters.
Blood dyscrasias: Risk of neutropenia, leukopenia, and agranulocytosis. Monitor CBC if symptoms or risk factors are present.
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Can lower blood pressure and increase fall risk, especially in older adults.
Hyperprolactinemia: Can cause amenorrhea, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, and possibly impact fertility.
Seizure risk: May lower seizure threshold; use caution in patients with seizure history, head trauma, or alcohol use disorder.
Hepatic and renal impairment: Contraindicated in liver damage and renal insufficiency; drug exposure may be unpredictable and toxicity risk increased.
patient_counseling: This is not a PRN anxiety pill. It is a long-term antipsychotic that needs consistent monitoring.
Tell your prescriber immediately if you notice chest pain, palpitations, fainting, or any history of long QT or serious heart problems.
Report new stiffness, shaking, inner restlessness, or abnormal movements early—do not wait for them to become severe.
Tell your clinician about changes in periods, breast changes, sexual side effects, or discharge from nipples.
Do not abruptly stop oral flupentixol without a plan—sudden discontinuation can cause withdrawal-like symptoms and relapse.
Elderly family members with dementia should generally not be placed on flupentixol unless there is a compelling safety reason and close monitoring.
Avoid dehydration, extreme heat, and heavy exertion until you know how this medicine affects your temperature regulation.
Let every prescriber know you are on an antipsychotic before they add other medications, especially heart medicines, antibiotics, or antidepressants.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most concerning: movement problems (EPS), cardiac conduction changes (QT prolongation, arrhythmias), hormonal changes from high prolactin, and rare but serious syndromes like NMS and blood dyscrasias.
plain_language_list: Movement side effects: Stiffness, tremor, inner restlessness, and abnormal movements (tardive dyskinesia).
Sedation and fatigue: Feeling sleepy, slowed, or mentally ‘foggy,’ though flupentixol is often somewhat less sedating than some other typicals.
Hormonal changes: Elevated prolactin leading to menstrual changes, breast changes, and sexual dysfunction.
Cardiac effects: Palpitations, QT prolongation, and risk of serious arrhythmias in vulnerable patients.
Metabolic changes: DKA, hyperglycemia, and weight changes.
GI symptoms: Constipation, dry mouth, nausea, and sometimes paralytic ileus.
Dermatologic reactions: Rashes, itching, and rare severe skin reactions.
Rare but life-threatening: NMS, severe blood count changes, and serious ventricular arrhythmias.

common.incidence: Up to ~30% depending on dose and vulnerability
common.patient_note: These are classic ‘stiff and shaky’ side effects: tremor, slowed movement, muscle rigidity, or painful muscle contractions. Akathisia feels like internal restlessness—you can’t sit still. Early detection is key; dose adjustments, adjunct meds, or switching agents may be needed.

common.incidence: Variable, often less sedating than some other typicals but still clinically significant
common.patient_note: You may feel sleepy or mentally slowed, especially when starting or after dose changes. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how you respond.

common.incidence: Not well quantified; reported depression, hypomania, psychomotor agitation, insomnia
common.patient_note: Some patients feel emotionally flat or depressed; others can feel more agitated or restless. Report mood changes promptly—this is not just ‘part of the illness’ and may need treatment changes.

common.incidence: Not precisely defined; hyperprolactinemia is a class effect
common.patient_note: Watch for missed periods, breast discharge, breast enlargement, low libido, or erectile problems. These can be medication-related and reversible if the treatment plan is adjusted.

common.incidence: Variable; flupentixol has relatively low anticholinergic potency but effects still occur
common.patient_note: Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary hesitancy or retention can occur. Severe constipation or belly pain needs urgent attention.

common.incidence: Not fully quantified; includes palpitations, syncope, QT prolongation
common.patient_note: Dizziness on standing, feeling like you might pass out, or a racing/irregular heartbeat should be reported urgently. Your clinician may order an ECG.

serious: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Fever, severe muscle rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability, elevated CPK, and possible kidney injury. This is a medical emergency and requires immediate discontinuation and hospital care.
Tardive dyskinesia: Involuntary, repetitive movements (tongue, lips, face, trunk, limbs) that can become irreversible, especially after long-term use in older adults and women.
Severe arrhythmias: Prolonged QT interval, torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and sudden cardiac death, particularly in high-risk patients.
Serious blood dyscrasias: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia. Symptoms may include fever, sore throat, infections, or unexplained bruising/bleeding.
Severe hepatic injury: Jaundice, markedly elevated AST/ALT or alkaline phosphatase, and clinical signs of liver dysfunction.
Severe dermatologic reactions: Exfoliative dermatitis or widespread rash with systemic symptoms.
Severe GI complications: Paralytic ileus with abdominal distension, pain, and absent bowel movements—requires urgent evaluation.
Venous thromboembolism: Deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism with leg swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Like other typical antipsychotics, flupentixol has important interactions via cardiac conduction, CNS depression, blood pressure, and seizure threshold. A full interaction check is essential before starting or changing doses.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (eg, certain antiarrhythmics, macrolide antibiotics, fluoroquinolones, methadone)
items.risk: Additive QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes or sudden death.
items.action: Avoid combinations when possible. If unavoidable, obtain baseline and follow-up ECGs, correct electrolytes, and use the lowest effective doses.

items.risk: Increased risk of EPS, NMS, hyperprolactinemia, and QT prolongation.
items.action: Avoid routine antipsychotic polypharmacy. If overlap is needed during switching, keep it brief and monitor closely for side effects.

items.with: CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, alcohol)
items.risk: Additive sedation, respiratory depression, impaired cognition, and falls.
items.action: Use lowest effective doses, avoid alcohol, and monitor for oversedation and respiratory compromise. In older adults, these combinations are particularly risky.

items.risk: Enhanced hypotension and dizziness, especially when standing.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure, particularly after starting or increasing flupentixol. Educate patients on slow position changes and fall risk.

items.with: Drugs that lower seizure threshold (eg, bupropion, tramadol, some antidepressants and stimulants)
items.risk: Increased risk of seizures, particularly in patients with seizure history or brain injury.
items.action: Use caution, avoid high doses, and consider alternatives if possible. Monitor for neurologic symptoms.

items.risk: Pharmacodynamic opposition—flupentixol blocks dopamine, potentially worsening Parkinsonian symptoms or reducing efficacy of dopaminergic treatment.
items.action: Avoid if possible in patients with Parkinson disease or those needing dopaminergic therapy. If used together, carefully balance benefits and motor side effects.

items.with: Strong CYP inhibitors or inducers (class effect caution)
items.risk: While specific CYP pathways are less emphasized clinically for flupentixol than for some atypicals, potent inducers or inhibitors may alter exposure.
items.action: When major CYP-modifying drugs are added or removed, monitor for loss of efficacy or increased side effects and adjust doses based on clinical response.

items.risk: Additive constipation, urinary retention, and blurred vision; may increase risk of heat illness.
items.action: Use with caution, especially in older adults or those with BPH, glaucoma, or chronic constipation.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping flupentixol needs a plan. With oral tablets, abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal-like symptoms and relapse. Depot formulations wear off slowly, so classic withdrawal is less of an issue, but relapse risk remains high if underlying illness is active.
key_points: Oral discontinuation: In chronic psychiatric illness, the default is usually to switch to another antipsychotic rather than fully stop. If the plan is to come off, taper gradually over weeks to months unless there’s a serious adverse effect that forces a quicker change.

Withdrawal symptoms: Abrupt oral discontinuation can cause agitation, anxiety, insomnia, alternating hot and cold sensations, sweating, restlessness, nausea, GI upset, myalgias, paresthesias, and worsening psychosis.

Taper pace (oral): A common strategy is to reduce the dose stepwise every 1–2 weeks, watching for early relapse or withdrawal. The exact schedule is individualized based on dose, duration of use, and risk level.
Depot discontinuation: Because the depot clears slowly, gradual dose reduction is usually not required to avoid withdrawal. The main risk is symptom recurrence as plasma levels fall.

Monitoring after stopping: Whether oral or depot, monitor closely for prodromal psychotic symptoms (sleep disturbance, subtle paranoia, social withdrawal, odd thinking) for weeks to months after discontinuation.

Switching antipsychotics: Cross-titration is often preferred—gradually lower flupentixol while slowly increasing the new antipsychotic. In high relapse-risk patients, there may be a period of overlap at full dose of the old agent while the new agent reaches therapeutic levels, followed by a slow taper off the old medication.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Flupentixol is usually started orally, then transitioned to a depot injection for maintenance once tolerability and response are established. Doses must be individualized and adjusted slowly based on clinical response and side effects.

adult.schizophrenia_oral_initial: 1 mg PO three times daily (total 3 mg/day).
adult.schizophrenia_oral_titration: Increase by 1 mg/day every 2–3 days based on response and tolerability.
adult.schizophrenia_oral_maintenance: Typical maintenance 3–6 mg/day in divided doses; doses ≥12 mg/day have been used in some patients but raise side-effect risk.
adult.schizophrenia_depot_initial_naive: IM depot test dose 5–20 mg once (5 mg recommended in elderly, frail, or EPS-prone patients). Monitor response and EPS over the next 5–10 days. Continue oral antipsychotic during overlap at a reduced dose, then taper off.
adult.schizophrenia_depot_initial_experienced: 20–40 mg IM as a first depot dose in patients with prior exposure and good tolerance to long-acting depot antipsychotics.
adult.schizophrenia_depot_maintenance: 20–40 mg IM 4–10 days after the initial injection, then 20–40 mg IM every 2–3 weeks. Titrate in increments of ≤20 mg; doses >80 mg are rarely needed.
adult.depot_conversion_from_oral_q2w: When converting from oral to depot every 2 weeks, use a decanoate dose approximately 4 times the total daily oral dose.
adult.depot_conversion_from_oral_q4w: When dosing depot every 4 weeks, use a decanoate dose approximately 8 times the total daily oral dose.
adult.depot_conversion_from_other_LAI: Approximate equivalence: flupentixol decanoate 40 mg ≈ fluphenazine decanoate 25 mg ≈ zuclopenthixol decanoate 200 mg ≈ haloperidol decanoate 50 mg.
adult.discontinuation_oral: If treatment must be stopped and the patient is not being switched to another antipsychotic, taper gradually over several weeks to months to reduce relapse and withdrawal symptoms, unless a serious adverse event requires more rapid discontinuation.
adult.discontinuation_depot: Tapering is generally not required when stopping depot injections due to slow elimination. Stop injections and monitor closely for symptom recurrence as levels decline over weeks.
adult.elderly: Start at the lower end of adult dosing (eg, 1 mg/day orally or a 5 mg depot test dose). Titrate slowly and use the minimum effective maintenance dose.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Use is contraindicated in liver damage. For milder hepatic dysfunction, use extreme caution, start low, and titrate slowly with close monitoring if used at all.
adult.renal_impairment: Use is contraindicated in renal insufficiency per product labeling, despite minimal renal clearance. Avoid in moderate to severe renal impairment.

sections.simple_explanation: In practice, we usually prove that someone can tolerate oral flupentixol first, then convert them to a depot injection every 2–3 weeks. The depot dose is calculated from the oral dose, and the oral medication is slowly tapered after the first injection. Doses must be individualized and adjusted slowly to balance symptom control with movement and other side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Flupentixol is a typical antipsychotic with limited modern pregnancy and lactation data. Decisions hinge on illness severity, prior medication response, and the risk of relapse if treatment is changed or stopped.
sections.pregnancy: Flupentixol crosses the placenta. As a class, first-generation antipsychotics have not shown a large increase in major congenital malformations overall, but individual data for flupentixol are limited. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can cause extrapyramidal or withdrawal symptoms in newborns (restlessness, feeding issues, abnormal tone, respiratory distress, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy solely to reduce neonatal symptoms is generally not recommended because relapse risk for the parent is high. If the patient is well-controlled on flupentixol and alternative options are limited or have failed, continuing at the lowest effective dose with close monitoring may be reasonable as part of a shared decision-making process.
sections.lactation: Flupentixol is present in breast milk at low concentrations. The manufacturer notes that adverse effects in nursing infants are unlikely at therapeutic maternal doses, but data are limited. If used during breastfeeding, monitor the infant for sedation, feeding difficulties, poor weight gain, or unusual movements. As always, balance the benefits of breastfeeding, the importance of maternal psychiatric stability, and the availability of alternative treatments.
sections.pediatrics: Safety and efficacy in children and adolescents are not established. Extrapyramidal symptoms, prolactin-related issues, and metabolic effects are concerns. This medication should generally be avoided in pediatric patients outside of specialized settings with strong justification and careful monitoring.
sections.geriatrics: Flupentixol is a high-risk medication in older adults. Antipsychotics in general are linked to higher stroke risk, cognitive decline, falls, and mortality, especially in dementia. It should not be used for behavioral symptoms of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options have failed and the patient poses a significant safety risk. If used (eg, for schizophrenia with long-standing psychosis), start at very low doses, titrate slowly, monitor sodium (risk of SIADH/hyponatremia), and reassess the need regularly.
sections.hepatic: Flupentixol is heavily hepatically metabolized and is contraindicated in liver damage. In any degree of hepatic impairment, use extreme caution if considered; in most cases, an alternative with a safer hepatic profile is preferred.
sections.renal: Product labeling both suggests no dose adjustment and lists renal insufficiency as a contraindication. Given predominant fecal excretion and limited data, best practice is to avoid flupentixol in clinically significant renal impairment and choose an alternative antipsychotic.
sections.other: In surgical patients on high-dose flupentixol, monitor closely for hypotension and interactions with anesthetics or other CNS depressants. For patients with prolactin-dependent tumors (eg, certain breast cancers), the prolactin-raising effect of flupentixol is a concern; consider alternatives that are more prolactin-sparing.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Adherence: Assess at every visit, especially in patients on oral therapy or who may miss depot appointments.
Mental status and psychotic symptoms: Track hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, mood, and functioning at every visit.

Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): Screen at each visit; use a rating scale (eg, for parkinsonism and akathisia) about 4 weeks after initiation or dose changes and at least annually, more often if high risk.

Tardive dyskinesia: Assess visually at every visit and complete a standardized rating scale (eg, AIMS) at least annually or every 6 months in high-risk groups (older adults, women, long-term exposure).
Fall risk: Reassess fall risk periodically, especially in adults ≥60 years or those with sedation, orthostasis, or gait impairment.
Vital signs: Monitor blood pressure (including orthostatics), heart rate, temperature, and signs of infection as clinically indicated.
ECG and cardiac status: Obtain baseline and follow-up ECG in patients with cardiovascular risk factors, existing heart disease, electrolyte abnormalities, or concurrent QT-prolonging drugs.
Weight, height, BMI, and waist circumference: Check weight and BMI at every visit for the first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually.
Metabolic labs: Fasting plasma glucose/HbA1c and lipid panel around 4 months after initiation and annually thereafter, or more often if abnormal.
Blood chemistries: Monitor electrolytes, renal function, liver function, and TSH as clinically indicated, especially in medically complex patients.
CBC: Check as clinically indicated, and more frequently in patients with low baseline WBC or a history of drug-induced leukopenia or neutropenia.
Prolactin and hormone-related symptoms: Ask at each visit about menstrual changes, libido, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, and sexual function; obtain prolactin levels if symptoms are present.
Ocular health: Eye examinations as clinically indicated, especially if visual symptoms arise or in patients at risk for ocular disease.
Metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular history: Periodically review personal and family history of obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.
Overall function and quality of life: Work, school, relationships, self-care, and independent living capacity should be routinely tracked to ensure the medication is helping more than it harms.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Flupentixol is available in Canada as oral tablets and as a long-acting intramuscular depot formulation. It is not marketed in the United States.
items: Oral tablets (Fluanxol): 0.5 mg, 3 mg.
IM depot solution (Fluanxol Depot): 20 mg/mL (1 mL ampoule); 100 mg/mL (1 mL ampoule).
Note: Excipient information may vary by manufacturer; always check the specific product labeling for details (including oil vehicle and potential allergens).

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Flupentixol is a thioxanthene-derivative, first-generation antipsychotic. It works primarily by blocking postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, dampening overactive dopamine pathways that drive hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. In simple terms, it turns down dopamine signaling in key circuits, which can quiet psychotic symptoms—but that same dopamine blockade also explains side effects like stiffness, tremor, and decreased motivation.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text:
From a modern psychiatry lens, flupentixol is an older, typical antipsychotic most relevant when you want a depot option and atypical choices are limited, poorly tolerated, or unavailable. It is not available in the US and is generally not first-line compared with second-generation antipsychotics, which usually have lower rates of extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia.

Typical use: stabilize the patient on an oral antipsychotic regimen (often flupentixol tablets), confirm tolerability, then transition to a depot injection every few weeks for maintenance. This strategy is particularly helpful when adherence to daily tablets is a challenge and the main goal is preventing relapse and rehospitalization.

Key tradeoffs: the depot can provide steady coverage and improve adherence, but typical antipsychotic side effects—EPS, prolactin elevation, and cardiac conduction risk—mean this is best handled by a psychiatrist with experience in long-acting injectable antipsychotics. Flupentixol is not an appropriate tool for catatonia, primary anxiety disorders, or behavioral symptoms in dementia unless there is a compelling safety justification and nonpharmacologic options have failed.

seo.title: Flupentixol (Fluanxol): Uses, Depot Dosing, Side Effects & Monitoring
seo.description: Flupentixol (Fluanxol) is a first-generation antipsychotic used mainly as a long-acting depot for schizophrenia. Learn about dosing, depot conversion, side effects (EPS, QT prolongation, prolactin), pregnancy and older adult considerations.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is flupentixol used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: Flupentixol is a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic used mainly for the long-term treatment of schizophrenia. It’s often used as a depot (long-acting) injection every few weeks to help keep symptoms under control and reduce relapse in people who have trouble taking daily pills. It is not an everyday anxiety or sleep medication and is not available in the United States.

faqs.q: Is flupentixol good for anxiety or insomnia?
faqs.a: No. Flupentixol is not an anxiety or sleep medication. It’s a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic meant for conditions like schizophrenia. Using it just for anxiety or insomnia would expose you to serious side effects, including movement disorders and heart rhythm changes, without a good risk–benefit ratio. If anxiety or insomnia are your main issues, your prescriber should look at safer, more targeted options.

faqs.q: How long does flupentixol take to work?
faqs.a: Oral flupentixol usually starts to show some benefit on agitation or psychotic symptoms within 1–2 weeks, with fuller improvement over 4–6 weeks. The depot injection starts working within 1–3 days of the shot and then releases the medication slowly for 2–4 weeks. This is a slow-and-steady medication, not a fast rescue drug.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between flupentixol tablets and Fluanxol Depot?
faqs.a: The tablets are taken by mouth, usually daily in divided doses, and are often used at the start of treatment to confirm tolerability and find the right dose. Fluanxol Depot is a long-acting intramuscular injection given every 2–3 weeks. The depot gives you more stable levels and helps if taking daily pills is tough, but it also means any side effects can last longer because the drug leaves your system slowly.

faqs.q: What are the most important side effects of flupentixol to watch for?
faqs.a: From a psychiatric standpoint, the big ones are movement side effects (stiffness, tremor, restlessness, abnormal facial or body movements), hormonal changes (missed periods, breast changes, sexual dysfunction), and cardiac conduction issues (QT prolongation, arrhythmias). You should also watch for mood changes (feeling overly flat or depressed), signs of NMS (fever, rigidity, confusion), and signs of low blood pressure or falls. Report any of these immediately.

Yes. Like other typical antipsychotics, flupentixol can cause tardive dyskinesia—late-onset, involuntary movements of the face, tongue, trunk, or limbs that can be persistent or even irreversible. The risk increases with higher doses, longer duration of treatment, older age, and in women. Regular movement checks are essential, and if early signs appear, your prescriber should reassess the medication and dose.

faqs.q: Is flupentixol safe in older adults or dementia?
faqs.a: All antipsychotics, including flupentixol, carry higher risks in older adults—stroke, cognitive decline, falls, and mortality. In dementia, antipsychotics are linked to increased death and are not approved for dementia-related psychosis. They should only be considered when non-drug strategies fail and the person is at serious risk of harming themselves or others. For late-onset schizophrenia or long-standing psychosis in an older adult, flupentixol may be used cautiously at low doses with frequent monitoring.

faqs.q: What about pregnancy and breastfeeding while on flupentixol?
faqs.a: Data for flupentixol itself are limited. As a class, older antipsychotics have not shown a large overall increase in major birth defects, but third-trimester exposure can cause newborn withdrawal or extrapyramidal symptoms (feeding issues, abnormal tone, irritability, breathing problems). Stopping an effective antipsychotic during pregnancy can be dangerous because relapse risk goes up. Decisions about continuing or changing flupentixol should be made with your psychiatrist and obstetric team, focusing on illness severity, past response, and your preferences. Flupentixol does pass into breast milk at low levels; if used while breastfeeding, the infant should be monitored for sedation and feeding issues.

faqs.q: How do you switch from another antipsychotic to flupentixol depot?
faqs.a: There’s no one perfect switching recipe. Typically, you’ll start by cross-titrating: slowly adding and increasing oral flupentixol while you gradually decrease the previous antipsychotic. Once you’re stable on an oral flupentixol dose, your clinician can calculate an approximate depot dose (often 4–8 times the daily oral dose, depending on injection interval), give a depot test dose, and overlap with a reduced oral dose for the first week or so. In high relapse-risk patients, a period of dual coverage may be used before tapering off the prior medication.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a flupentixol depot injection?
faqs.a: Because the depot leaves your system slowly, you won’t crash immediately, but your protection fades over days to weeks. Psychotic symptoms—sleep disruption, subtle paranoia, hearing voices more often—can quietly creep back. If you miss an injection, contact your clinic as soon as possible. Your prescriber will decide whether to give the usual dose, adjust timing or dose, or temporarily add oral medication, depending on how late you are and how you’re feeling.

faqs.q: Why would someone choose flupentixol instead of a newer atypical antipsychotic?
faqs.a: In many systems, second-generation antipsychotics are preferred first because they usually have fewer movement side effects. Flupentixol sometimes enters the picture when a patient has done well on it historically, has limited access to atypicals, or needs a specific depot option that fits their context. It can be a reasonable choice when the benefits for a particular person outweigh the risks, but it’s not a modern ‘go-to’ for first-line treatment in most guidelines.
